# The Town of Three Clocks

In Marrow Bend there were three clocks, and none of them agreed.

The first stood on the courthouse, a great pale face with iron hands, and it ran eleven minutes fast. The second hung in the train station, though no train had stopped there in thirty years. It ran slow, and nobody could say by how much, because it slowed a little more each winter. The third was a wristwatch, worn by a woman named Odalys Prewitt, who insisted it was correct and dared anyone to prove otherwise.

Nobody could. That was the trouble.

---

I came to Marrow Bend in October, hired to survey the old canal for a company that would never build anything there. That was the polite fiction of the job. What they really wanted was a report that said *no*, and I was the sort of person who could write one without lingering.

The woman at the boarding house, a broad, quiet person named Ines, gave me a key and a warning. "Don't ask anyone what time it is," she said. "Ask them when they're having supper."

"Why?"

"Because then you'll get an answer you can use."

I thought it was a joke. It wasn't.

---

By the third day I understood the system, if it could be called that. The courthouse clock governed the official world, so court, the post office, and the bank all opened by its eleven-minutes-ahead time. Everyone knew this and quietly subtracted eleven. It was like knowing a friend always exaggerates.

The station clock governed the old men, who gathered beneath it each morning on a bench worn smooth as a river stone. They said they kept to "station time" out of loyalty, but I think it was something gentler. A clock that runs down slowly is a clock that lets you off easy. Under it, nobody was ever quite late.

And Odalys Prewitt's watch governed Odalys Prewitt, and by extension anyone unlucky enough to have an appointment with her.

I met her at the canal, where she stood on the towpath with her arms folded, watching me measure the silt.

"You're twelve minutes behind," she said.

"Behind what?"

"Today." She tapped the watch. It was a small, scratched thing on a cracked leather band. "I've been here since seven."

"I didn't know we had an appointment."

"We didn't. But you're behind anyway."

I liked her immediately.

---

Over the next week she followed me along the canal, correcting my measurements, my posture, and my pronunciation of the town's name. It was *Marrow*, as in bone, not *Marro*, as in the flavor. She had been a surveyor herself once, she said, before the canal dried and the company left and the town settled into its permanent disagreement with itself.

"Do you actually believe your watch is right?" I asked one evening. We were sitting on the lock wall with our feet over the dry channel, where a little water still pooled in the low places and held the sky.

She looked at it a long moment. "I believe it's *mine*," she said. "That's different. And better."

"How so?"

"Right is a thing you have to keep checking. Mine is a thing I just have." She almost smiled. "My husband gave me this. It's lost four seconds a year since 1987. I've never once corrected it. So when it's wrong, it's wrong in a way I recognize. It's wrong like a person is wrong. Consistently, and with affection."

I didn't know what to say to that, so I wrote down a silt measurement.

---

On my last night, Ines made supper at what she called "seven, more or less," and the more or less was the whole point. The old men from the station came, and a clerk from the courthouse, and Odalys, who arrived exactly when she said she would, which by everyone else's reckoning was either early or late depending on whose clock you trusted.

We ate. Someone told a story about a flood. Someone else corrected the story. The clerk laughed at the wrong moment and everyone forgave him.

Around nine, or nine-eleven, or a quarter to, the talk turned to me.

"What will you write?" asked the oldest of the men, a gaunt fellow named Tobiah who hadn't spoken all week.

"That the canal can't be restored," I said. "That it would cost more than the town is worth."

Nobody argued. They nodded like people hearing a diagnosis they had already guessed.

"Is that true?" Tobiah asked.

"The numbers are true."

"That's not what I asked."

I looked around the table at the mismatched faces, lit by the kitchen bulb. Somewhere outside, three clocks were telling three stories about the same night, and none of them was lying.

"I don't know," I said finally. "I think the numbers can't measure what's here."

"What's here?" Ines said gently.

"Agreement," I said. "Not about the time. About *each other*. You've all decided that being slightly wrong together is better than being exactly right alone."

The table was quiet. Then Odalys Prewitt reached over, took my wrist, and looked at my watch, a sleek, dutiful, satellite-synced thing.

"Twelve minutes behind," she said, and let go.

But she was smiling.

---

I wrote the report on the train out, on a different line from a different town, since Marrow Bend's station had no service. It said what I was hired to say. The canal could not be restored. The numbers were the numbers.

But in the margin of the last page, in pencil, where no one at the company would ever look, I wrote: *There is a town here that keeps three kinds of time. Consider what it would cost to lose all three.*

Then I set my watch back eleven minutes, then forward eleven, then back again, trying to find which felt like home.

None of them did. Not yet. But I noticed, somewhere between one station and the next, that I was no longer in a hurry to know.

Outside the window, the fields went by at exactly the speed they wanted to.
